lesson.title: The Body's Nightlight Switch: Melatonin and the Sleep Wake Cycle
lesson.summary: Melatonin is a hormone released by the pineal gland that helps regulate the body's circadian rhythm, rising in darkness to promote sleepiness and falling with light exposure. It is one of the clearest examples of how the endocrine system keeps behavior synchronized with the natural cycle of day and night.
lesson.body:
Melatonin is produced by the pineal gland, a small structure deep within the brain, but its release is not simply a matter of the gland acting on its own schedule. It is directly driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, a region of the hypothalamus that functions as the body's master circadian clock, tying melatonin production tightly to the central nervous system's own internal timing signals rather than to the pineal gland alone.

The suprachiasmatic nucleus receives direct input from the retina about ambient light levels, giving the brain a continuous readout of whether it is light or dark outside. In darkness, the suprachiasmatic nucleus signals the pineal gland to increase melatonin secretion, and melatonin then circulates through the body and brain, binding receptors that promote drowsiness and help prepare the body for sleep. When light, especially light in the blue wavelength range, strikes the retina, the suprachiasmatic nucleus suppresses melatonin release, helping to keep the person more alert. This light dependent on and off pattern is what keeps the body's internal circadian rhythm roughly synchronized with the twenty four hour day night cycle.

Melatonin does not work like a sedative that forces sleep to occur. It functions more like a timing signal, essentially announcing to the rest of the body that it is nighttime, which shifts the timing of numerous other physiological processes, including body temperature and other hormone release patterns, to align with an expected period of sleep. Because of this broader signaling role, disrupting melatonin timing through irregular light exposure can throw the whole system out of sync even for someone who is technically getting enough total hours of sleep.

Jet lag offers a familiar example of this disruption in action. Crossing several time zones puts a traveler's internal melatonin rhythm out of step with the new location's actual light and dark cycle, contributing to daytime fatigue and nighttime wakefulness until the internal clock gradually resets itself over the following days. Some travelers use carefully timed melatonin supplements to help nudge that internal clock forward or backward more quickly. Night shift workers face a related challenge, since regular exposure to light during what would normally be nighttime hours often leaves their melatonin release chronically suppressed or mistimed, contributing to persistent sleep difficulties even outside of any travel.

Everyday screen use illustrates the same mechanism on a smaller scale. Light emitted by phones, tablets, and computer screens, particularly blue wavelength light similar to daylight, activates the same retinal pathway that signals the suprachiasmatic nucleus to suppress melatonin. Using bright screens late at night can therefore delay the natural rise in melatonin and push back the point at which a person starts to feel genuinely sleepy, which is one reason sleep hygiene recommendations commonly suggest dimming screens or switching to warmer color settings in the hour or so before bed.
